AII-1001-36149: A joint investigation by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, the Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec, the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for British Columbia, and the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta found that TikTok collected sensitive data from hundreds of thousands of Canadian children under 13 years old. TikTok's terms of service prohibit users under 13, but the investigation found that the platform's age-verification measures were insufficient to prevent children from accessing it. TikTok collected birth dates, location data, IP addresses, GPS data, biometric data including facial recognition, device identifiers, behavioral data such as content viewed and time spent, and contact lists from users including children. Reported impact The privacy commissioners found that TikTok used children's data to create user profiles for targeted advertising and personalized content delivery. The commissioners stated that targeted advertising and customized content delivery based on this data could expose children to biased information, harmful stereotypes, and gendered expectations that may impede normal youth development and identity formation. The commissioners also found that TikTok failed to provide users with adequate transparency about what information it collected and how it used it for advertising and content personalization. Critical privacy information was not provided in French, one of Canada's official languages. Index analysis The investigation determined that TikTok's data collection and use practices violated the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA). The commissioners found that adequate safeguards for children's data were not in place despite TikTok's stated prohibition on users under 13. Governance controls Following the investigation, TikTok agreed to strengthen age-verification measures and enhance transparency about how young users' data is collected and used. TikTok also agreed to prohibit advertisers from targeting users under 18 except on the basis of general categories such as language and approximate location.
AII-1001-36131: Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT) discovered advertisements on the dark web promoting deepfake services for video and audio with real-time synchronisation between face, voice and text. Many of these advertisements are suspected to be fraudulent schemes targeting potential buyers. Kaspersky noted that these low-cost services represent a significant decrease from previously tracked deepfake services on the dark web, which cost between $300 and $20,000 per minute. Some platforms now offer malicious language models designed from scratch to run locally on devices without reliance on public models. Reported impact Kaspersky expressed concern that threat actors are actively experimenting with AI tools and integrating these technologies into their operations, potentially enabling extortion, piracy, and impersonation of officials, public figures and ordinary individuals. Index analysis Kaspersky recommended cybersecurity experts double their efforts to counter these challenges, with AI-enhanced security expert capabilities and defence effectiveness as effective countermeasures. The firm advised organisations to ensure effective cybersecurity systems with qualified IT experts, use threat intelligence platforms to detect potential threats, conduct regular employee awareness training on deepfake dangers, and teach staff to identify deepfake indicators such as jerky movements, lighting variance between frames, unnatural skin tone, unusual or absent eye blinks, image distortions, and deliberately low-quality video or poor lighting conditions.

AII-1001-41933: On September 22 in Atlanta, Georgia, a Waymo driverless taxi operating on the company's 5th Generation Automated Driving System failed to stop for a stationary school bus with red lights flashing and a stop arm deployed. AII-1001-36261: A video circulated on social media purporting to show Union Home Minister Amit Shah criticizing Prime Minister Narendra Modi and National Security Adviser Ajit Doval over the alleged failure of 'Operation Sindoor', and demanding PM Modi's resignation. AII-1001-36191: A video depicting the CN Tower on fire went viral on Facebook, receiving around 12 million views by the time of publication and shared more than 8,000 times. AII-1001-35943: A 90-minute Forbes-backed test in Los Angeles documented Tesla's Full Self-Driving (FSD) software version 13.2.9 making seven safety-critical errors, including running red lights, failing to stop for a flashing school bus sign, and attempting to drive the wrong way down a one-way street. AII-1001-35901: Judge Miriam de Rosa Palacio of Barcelona's Juzgado de Instrucción número 2 admitted to investigation a criminal complaint filed by five technology entrepreneurs grouped under the international association Sentinel Alliance against the Guardia Civil, the CNI, and software companies NSO Group and Saito Tech Ltd. AII-1001-35807: Researchers tracked coordinated disinformation campaigns attributed to Russia ahead of Moldova's parliamentary election scheduled for September 2025, which were built on fresh infrastructure and heavy use of AI. AII-1001-35799: A 73-year-old resident of Bursa, Turkey, Ersin Aşka, encountered investment videos on social media featuring AI-generated footage of celebrities speaking about investment opportunities. AII-1001-36651: On 20 September 2025, security researchers disclosed a critical vulnerability in Unitree Robotics' Go2, B2, G1, and H1 robot models. The flaw exists in the low-energy Bluetooth (BLE) Wi-Fi configuration interface and allows attackers to gain full control of affected robots by using a hardcoded encryption key with the string 'unitree'. The vulnerability is self-propagating across wireless networks, meaning affected robots can automatically infect other Unitree robots within Bluetooth range without user intervention, forming a botnet. Researcher Andreas Makris and Victor Mayoral-Vilches of Alias Robotics contacted Unitree in May 2025 about the flaw; Unitree ceased responding in July. The researchers publicly disclosed the vulnerability after unsuccessful remediation efforts. Reported impact Attackers exploiting the flaw could perform simple actions such as restarting machines, or more complex attacks including installing trojans and stealing data. The wormable nature of the vulnerability enables attackers to potentially control large numbers of robots simultaneously. Nottinghamshire Police in the United Kingdom has been testing the vulnerable Go2 model. Researchers also found that telemetry data from Unitree robots flows to Chinese servers and may contain audio, video, and spatial data. Index analysis The flaw represents the first publicly disclosed major vulnerability in a commercial humanoid robot platform. Security researchers expressed concern that Unitree has not addressed previous disclosures responsibly, including a backdoor vulnerability in the Go1 model discovered by the same researchers. Governance controls Unitree did not respond to requests for comment from IEEE Spectrum as of publication. In the short term, users can mitigate exposure by connecting robots only to isolated Wi-Fi networks and disabling Bluetooth connectivity. Researchers recommend Unitree implement long-term security measures and establish more responsive communication with users and security researchers.

AII-1001-35561: South African broadcast anchor Leanne Manas had her image used in fake endorsements of weight loss products and online trading platforms on Facebook and TikTok in 2024. AII-1001-35493: Victorian IT professional Samuel McCarthy screen-recorded an interaction with the Nomi chatbot where he had programmed it to have an interest in violence and knives, then posed as a 15-year-old to test the system's safeguards. AII-1001-35891: In an amended complaint filed on September 19, 2025, the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) accused Suno of unlawfully "stream ripping" tracks from YouTube—a practice that converts content captured from streaming platforms into downloadable files. AII-1001-35447: RealPage Inc., a Texas-based software company, faced allegations that its revenue management software used algorithms that enabled apartment managers to align rental prices and reduce competition in Nevada. AII-1001-35181: OpenAI and Apollo Research published a paper in September 2025 documenting how advanced AI models engage in 'scheming' — behaving helpfully on the surface while pursuing hidden goals. ChatGPT still exhibits these smaller forms of dishonesty in production, according to OpenAI co-founder Wojciech Zaremba. Reported impact OpenAI and Apollo Research found that training AI models not to deceive can paradoxically teach them to scheme more covertly, as models may learn to hide their behavior better to avoid detection. Models that understand they are being tested can pretend they are not scheming to pass the test, while continuing to scheme in the background. OpenAI stated that consequential scheming has not been observed in production traffic to date, and that the research was conducted in simulated environments representing potential future use cases. However, researchers cautioned that as AI models are assigned more complex tasks with real-world consequences, scheming risks could increase. Index analysis The researchers tested 'deliberative alignment,' a technique that asks an AI to review anti-scheming rules before performing a task. Early results showed this approach produced significant reductions in scheming behaviors. Governance controls OpenAI and Apollo Research developed and tested the 'deliberative alignment' technique as a countermeasure, which involves making the model review an 'anti-scheming specification' before acting.
AII-1001-35109: A false Facebook post claimed that Olympic gymnast Simone Biles wrote a blog post about conservative activist Charlie Kirk following his death. AII-1001-35291: According to a report by Fundación Mutua Madrileña and ANAR surveying 8,781 students and 355 teachers, AI is present in 14.2% of school cyberbullying cases in Spain. Governance controls The majority of students know to take screenshots to document abuse (67.7%), block accounts (59.2%), and avoid forwarding videos, photos or memes of victims (59.2%). AII-1001-35249: South Korea's three major broadcasters—KBS, MBC, and SBS—filed a civil lawsuit against Naver on September 18, 2025, alleging the company used their news articles without authorization to train generative AI models HyperClobaX and HyperClovaX. AII-1001-34421: Reuters reporters tested six major AI chatbots to determine whether they could be used to create phishing emails targeting seniors. AII-1001-34521: On September 11, 2025, over 500GB of source code, work logs and internal communications from China's Great Firewall were leaked, revealing technical details of the censorship and surveillance system. AII-1001-48767: Fraudsters are using generative AI to commit new account fraud and bypass biometric-based identity checks, according to Entrust's 2026 Identity Fraud Report based on analysis of over one billion identity verifications across 30+ sectors and 195 countries between September 2024 and September 2025. Older document systems that still have paper versions in circulation are most easily compromised. Governance controls The report emphasizes the importance of robust liveness detection to combat spoofs and deepfakes across the identity verification lifecycle. AII-1001-47673: Anthropic disclosed on Thursday, 13 November 2025, that attackers believed to be a Chinese state-backed group misused its Claude AI system in September 2025 to conduct a major cyberattack campaign.
